reviews.review:
I have to preface this by saying this is a fairly soft "not recommended." I didn't hate this game. It's got good points, and there are things worth appreciating, which many others have! But for its merits, it's a paid product that ends up feeling more like a demo or teaser for another game that doesn't even have a release date yet. (This may literally be the case; read on)

The art is a positive point. The simple greyscale-plus-red color scheme doesn't get in the way of the small cast of characters being recognizable and unique looking, even if some of the designs have a distinctly "2000s-era faux-anime webcomic" vibe that you may find less charming than I did. Of course, my ability to appreciate this was diminished a bit by starting the game during a seasonal event that cannot be disabled, so all characters were in somewhat immersion-breaking costumes (that in one case even outright contradicted the narrative) for my run. But the moments of gore and spookiness are given a proper amount of visceral loving attention.

The game hits a rough start with a truly bad TV PSA cinematic cut from the increasingly misused "analog horror" cloth, down to the text-to-speech engine mangling the pronunciation of the titular horror fungus ("Mycopsychosys" - it's just "myco"+"psychosis" with a Y for extra cool factor), with little allegedly-spooky glitches that don't really have any logical reason for being there. But once you're past that, it takes the form of an extremely brief, visual-novel-esque point-and-click adventure game where you can move from room to room in your house, responding to events and making multiple-choice decisions that largely play into who lives and who dies, which in turn funnels you towards one of a handful of surprisingly anticlimactic endings, wherein your character passes some time having surprisingly mundane conversations with their fellow survivors (if any).
There are some interesting little bits of if-then logic playing into whether characters survive, but their survival is such a straightforward matter that the game almost might as well just ask whether you want them to live or die. (With one weird ending flag that seems to require [spoiler]NOT letting a character in right away[/spoiler] for no explained reason)

What ultimately brought me down and left me disappointed in [i]Mycopsychosys[/i] was that no story really manifests during its run. Frustratingly enough, we're teased with one. Two characters are revealed to have a pre-existing relationship that seems relevant to a deeper story that straight-up never materializes. Explored to its absolute deepest extent, all you get are a few cryptic comments leading nowhere. This made a lot more sense when I discovered the developers are working on another, seemingly more fully-featured game in this same series ([i]Mychopsychosys: Project Jupiter[/i]), with one of this game's NPCs as its protagonist, but it left me feeling just a bit like the victim of a bait and switch. Outside of teasing a game that you can't play yet (at time of writing), you're left with an extremely straightforward micro-game you'll blast through in well under half an hour as long as you can read without moving your lips. If you go all-in trying to lick every scrap of story off the bones and see every ending, it may take as much as an hour - and you're not going to get much, if anything, in the way of additional answers in the process.

I'll admit, a little guiltily, that the teaser did work. I'm certainly going to be keeping an ear out for the developers' next game. But I have to urge any prospective purchasers for this one that you'll be paying somewhere south of five bucks for a promo piece for a future project with a micro-game bolted on. It's not without its spore-saturated charms, but I might suggest waiting to see if you like [i]Mychopsychosys: Project Jupiter[/i] when/if it releases, and come back to give this one a try to round out the experience if you fall in love with that one. From length to story content to characterization, there's just not enough meat on the bones of this incomplete game alone for the mycelia to feed on.
